passage: Creche note, Tuesday. Around midday, Farhan, two, began rubbing his eyes with both fists and tugging his left ear. He also pressed his face into my shoulder. I didn't decide from one sign. It was just before nap time, he had eaten his lunch well, he felt cool to touch, and the room had been noisy since morning. I took him to the quiet corner and he slept. If the ear-tugging keeps going or worries us, I will tell his parents to see the doctor. 🙂 Ganga

qa.q: When did Farhan start rubbing his eyes and tugging his ear?
qa.a: Around midday, just before nap time.

qa.q: What might Farhan have been feeling when he rubbed his eyes and tugged his ear, and how did Ganga decide?
qa.a: He was most likely tired, since it was just before nap time and he pressed his face into Ganga's shoulder, and Ganga checked the whole picture: lunch eaten, cool skin and a noisy room. The ear tug could have another cause, so Ganga will watch whether it continues.

qa.q: What should Ganga do if the ear tugging continues?
qa.a: Ganga should tell his parents so they can check with the doctor, since it may be more than tiredness.

qa.q: How might Farhan's parents feel on reading the note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that Ganga looked carefully and told them, and know what to watch for.

grounding: A toddler rubs his eyes and pulls his ear, an ambiguous cue that the caregiver checks against the whole situation.

passage: The bus ride from town had taken all afternoon, and by the evening meal Avni, two, was tugging at her right ear and rubbing her eyes with her fists. Jomon looked at her: she had eaten little, the radio was loud and she had been awake since dawn. He turned the radio off, lifted her on his lap and rocked her. She pressed her face into his shirt and was asleep in a few minutes. He decided that if the tugging carried on the next day, he would ask the clinic nurse.

qa.q: What did Jomon switch off?
qa.a: The radio.

qa.q: What did Jomon think Avni's ear tugging and eye rubbing meant?
qa.a: He thought she was tired after the long bus ride, since she had eaten little and been awake since dawn. He still kept in mind that ear tugging can have other causes.

qa.q: What would Jomon do if the tugging kept going?
qa.a: He would ask the clinic nurse the next day, as it might be something more than tiredness.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when he turned off the radio?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved as the noise stopped, and safe in his lap. 🙂

grounding: A toddler rubs eyes and tugs an ear when sleepy, and an adult checks the wider context instead of relying on one sign.

passage:
At a pavement café in Barcelona, Xin started rubbing her eyes with both fists and pushing her face into Lucia's chest.
"Sleepy already?" Lucia checked the time. Xin had napped well that morning. The street was quiet. But lunch had been small and early.
Lucia took a rice cake from her bag. Xin grabbed it, ate it in four bites, and sat up straight, bright-eyed, pointing at the pigeons.

qa.q: What did Lucia take from her bag?
qa.a: A rice cake.

qa.q: What was Xin most likely feeling when she rubbed her eyes, and what else might it have been?
qa.a: She was most likely hungry, since she perked up after eating; it could also have been tiredness, but Xin had napped well that morning, so Lucia ruled that out.

qa.q: Which choice of Lucia's worked, and why?
qa.a: Checking the nap, the noise and the lunch before deciding worked, because it led her to the real need, hunger.

qa.q: What would change if Lucia had assumed Xin was sleepy?
qa.a: She might have tried to put her down for a rest, and Xin would have stayed hungry and fussy.

grounding: A mother reads her toddler's eye-rubbing by checking nap, noise and food, and finds hunger rather than sleep.

passage: I'm Tarun, and I thought my little brother Mohit was just sleepy that evening. He kept tugging his right ear and rubbing his eyes, and he pushed his face into Mummy's neck. But it was only six o'clock. Mummy felt his forehead and cheeks and said he was warm. She didn't wait to see. She rang the doctor that evening and took him in. I was wrong about the sleepy part. You can't tell from one sign.

qa.q: Which ear did Mohit keep tugging?
qa.a: His right ear.

qa.q: What was Mohit likely feeling as he tugged his ear and pushed his face into Mummy's neck?
qa.a: He was likely unwell and uncomfortable, perhaps in pain, and wanted comfort; tiredness was possible, but it was early and he felt warm.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that was wise?
qa.a: She checked the whole picture, the time and his warm forehead, and rang the doctor that same evening instead of waiting.

qa.q: How does Tarun see the evening afterwards?
qa.a: Tarun realises the first guess was wrong and learns that one sign isn't enough to know what's going on.

grounding: A brother learns that his toddler brother's ear-tugging and eye-rubbing meant feeling unwell, as their mother checked the whole picture.

passage:
Monday, one o'clock: Kalyani rubbed her eyes and leaned on Vikas's leg. It was nap time. He took her to bed and she slept at once.
Thursday, at a loud birthday party: she rubbed her eyes again and hid her face. It wasn't nap time. Vikas carried her out to the quiet hallway, and she brightened.
Saturday evening, dinner was late: eye-rubbing, whining. Vikas gave her a banana, and she stopped.

qa.q: What did Vikas give Kalyani on Saturday evening?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling each time she rubbed her eyes?
qa.a: On Monday she was tired, on Thursday overwhelmed by the loud party, and on Saturday hungry; the same cue carried different feelings.

qa.q: What habit helped Vikas respond well?
qa.a: He looked at the time, the place and what she had eaten each time, rather than assuming one meaning.

qa.q: What would change if Vikas had always put Kalyani to bed when she rubbed her eyes?
qa.a: He would have missed that she was overwhelmed or hungry on other days, and she would have stayed upset.

grounding: Over a week a father learns that his toddler's eye-rubbing can mean tired, overwhelmed or hungry, and checks the whole picture.

passage:
A wedding band was thumping in the lane below the Jaipur flat. Mehak rubbed her eyes with both fists, then tugged at her left ear and pushed her face into Gargi's kurta.
Gargi ran through it. Dinner, eaten. Forehead, not hot. Nap, too short. And that band.
She shut the window, dimmed the lights and started rocking her.
If the ear-tugging kept going or worried her, she'd check with the doctor. For now, Mehak's eyes were closing.

qa.q: Which ear did Mehak tug at?
qa.a: She tugged at her left ear.

qa.q: What was Mehak most likely feeling when she rubbed her eyes and tugged her ear?
qa.a: She was most likely tired and a bit overwhelmed by the band's noise; the same cues could have meant hunger or feeling unwell, which is why Gargi checked.

qa.q: What did Gargi do that a careful caregiver would copy?
qa.a: She checked the whole picture, food, temperature, nap and noise, before deciding, and planned to see the doctor if the ear-tugging kept going or worried her.

qa.q: How did Gargi likely feel as Mehak's eyes closed?
qa.a: Gargi likely felt relieved that tiredness and noise were the probable cause.

grounding: It shows a toddler rubbing her eyes and tugging her ear, an ambiguous cue, and a caregiver checking the whole picture rather than one sign.
